issues.body: reified_provenance mints the anchor from (subject, predicate, object, rule) but attribution_triples also attaches bridgedFromPolicy. Rule identifiers are not guaranteed globally unique: anonymous rules are represented by blank-node-label strings and programmatic ids are explicitly supported. If two policies with different IRIs emit the same grant and reuse the same rule id/blank-node label, both materializations mint the same anchor; deduplication then leaves that anchor linked to both policies. Audit queries can no longer determine which rule-policy pair produced the grant, contradicting the originating-policy and separate-attribution claims. The existing two_rules_stay_separately_attributable test uses different triples and different rule IRIs, so it does not exercise this collision.
issues.fix_hint: Include a collision-safe policy identity in the plain-grant anchor key, with an explicit representation for policies without an IRI, or otherwise mint a source-instance identity that preserves rule-policy pairs. Add a real-path regression test that materializes the same auth triple from two distinct policies whose rules share the same blank-node/programmatic id, then verifies distinct anchors and unambiguous rule-to-policy attribution across rematerialization/refresh. Review the analogous conditional-grant shape-key collapse and either preserve rule-policy pairing there too or document/test the intended many-source model.
issues.title: Reification anchors collide across policies

verdict.summary: Round 2 introduces a provenance-identity collision not covered by the tests. Plain-grant reification anchors are keyed only by the emitted triple and rule identifier, while each anchor also carries a policy identifier. Two policies can therefore produce the same auth triple with the same non-global rule id (especially repeated blank-node labels or programmatic ids), causing their provenance to collapse onto one RDF statement and making rule-to-policy attribution ambiguous. The implementation and documentation claim originating-policy attribution and separate attribution, so this must be fixed or explicitly modeled before approval. Because round 1 had no findings, this is regressing.
